title: Campaign Readiness Check
subtitle: Before We Continue
martuIntro:
Before the campaign goes on, show me what you can do on your own. This is practice, never a grade.
Part 1: twelve questions, then nine short tasks, with no hints. Part 2: the mini-boss, a whole campaign part with only the help the campaign gives. Then one click: explain a line you wrote.
Missed something? The page *Mar'tu's Notes: Where to Look Again* shows which lesson to open.
Once, this code was a wall. Now you take it apart yourself, yes?
goals: Read every line of the code a campaign part starts with, and say what it does
Make small campaign changes with no hints: replace `pass`, store a result and pass it on, change a stat sheet, roll a die
Read Python's error message and fix the line it points to
Finish a whole campaign part with only the campaign's help: hold the ward with `if`, `elif` and `else`
Explain a line you wrote, in plain words

items.title: Before We Continue
items.summary: What the Readiness Check is, and how it works. Practice, never a grade.
items.body:
Mar'tu: Before the campaign goes on, show me what you can do on your own. This is practice, never a grade.
You played the campaign's first two modules, and a lot of that code felt like a wall. Since then, you took the wall apart, one stone at a time.
1. Part 1: twelve questions, then nine short tasks. Hints are off. The glossary, read-aloud and the error box in the Console still work. Stuck on a task? Type your best try, press Run once, then skip it and come back later. Tasks you pass stay ✓ done.
2. Part 2, the mini-boss: hold the Lantern Ward, a spell that protects, with only the help the campaign gives: the numbered comments, the check messages, the error box, and my version after 5 minutes. That is [[campaign mode]].
3. Then one click: explain a line you wrote.
Missed something? Open *Mar'tu's Notes: Where to Look Again*, right after Part 1. A miss only shows us which lesson to look at again, together. The story goes on either way.
You have learned enough to help, yes? Show me without the hints. Then we continue.
About 45 minutes.

items.title: Readiness Check · Part 1 · Form A questions
items.summary: Part 1 starts here: twelve questions about what code prints, which line runs, and what a line means. No hints. Then come nine short tasks.

questions.q: What will this code print?
questions.explain: `str(7)` and `str(10)` turn the numbers into text. Then `+` glues the pieces like a compound word, with no spaces added. The only space is the one inside `"Mana: "`.

questions.q: `get_warning()` tidies its line with `.lower()`, then `.capitalize()`. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the very first letter big. It is not like sentence case in Google Docs: names and new sentences get no capital, so even Lucky's name stays small.

questions.q: `latch_check` passes when the roll is at least 11. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*, like the filled dot on a number line: 11 itself counts. 10 is short, so `False`. 11 is exactly enough, so `True`. 12 is more than enough, so `True`.

questions.q: Trace this program like a ledger: write down what each variable holds, one line at a time, the way you show your work in math. Then type the number it prints.
questions.explain:
Here is the same kind of trace for another call, `lamp_glow(1, 2) + 8`. `oil` gets 1 and `wicks` gets 2, so `light` is 10 and `spark` is 8. The call hands back 18, and the line adds 8, so it prints 26. Trace yours the same way, with what is *in* the variables.
If you got 22, you added the numbers written in the function, 10 + 4, then the 8. If you got 16, you added the numbers handed over, 3 + 5, then the 8.

questions.q: `choice` holds `"option 2"`. What will this code print?
questions.explain: Python checks the chain from the top and stops at the first question that is `True`, like a grading scale. `choice == "option 1"` is `False`, so it skips that branch. `choice == "option 2"` is `True`, so `Gearshift goes.` prints, and Python skips the rest of the chain.

questions.q: `in` asks about a dictionary's keys. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `in` looks only at the keys, the way you check a glossary for a word, not for its meaning. `"Glow"` is a key, so `True`. 2 is a value, not a key, so `False`.

questions.q: What will this code print?
questions.explain: Text times a number repeats it, the way 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4: three `█`, then two `░`, glued together with no spaces.

questions.q: Which numbers can `random.randint(1, 6)` give?

whyWrong.0: That is what `range(1, 6)` gives, which stops before 6. `randint` can give both ends.
whyWrong.1: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0.
whyWrong.3: Every whole number from 1 to 6 can come up, not only the two ends.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 6)` rolls like a fair d6, a die with 6 faces: any whole number from 1 to 6, and both 1 and 6 can come up.

questions.q: Which sentence says what `spells["glow"]` and `spells["glow"](pell)` each do?
choices: Both run the spell on Pell.
The first is the function itself, not run. The second runs it on Pell.
The first runs the spell. The second stores Pell in the book.
The first is the word glow. The parentheses turn it into a function.

whyWrong.0: Only parentheses after it, like `(pell)`, run a function. `spells["glow"]` on its own only reads it.
whyWrong.2: Nothing is stored: `(pell)` hands Pell to the function and runs it.
whyWrong.3: The value under the key `"glow"` is the function `glow`, not text.

questions.explain: In math class, f names a function and f(3) works it out. In the same way, `spells["glow"]` reads the function stored under `"glow"` without running it, and `(pell)` on the end runs it on Pell.

questions.q: Here is the same spell book. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `found = spells["glow"]` stores the function itself, so `found(pell)` runs it on Pell: one line. The last line only reads the function, with no parentheses after it, so nothing more prints. It is like writing f without (3): you named the function, but you didn't use it.

questions.q: Trace the loop one hero at a time. What will this code print?
questions.explain: The loop takes the heroes one at a time, in order, like a teacher calling roll. Each time through, `show_status` prints one line: Moss 3, then Pell 7, then Brakka 9.

questions.q: What do the last two lines, the `for` loop, do?
choices: It calls `show_status` once, with the whole roster.
It calls `show_status` three times, with the whole roster each time.
It makes three new functions, one for each hero.
It calls `show_status` three times, once with each hero's sheet.

whyWrong.0: The indented line under `for` runs once for each item in the list, so there are three calls, not one.
whyWrong.1: Each time through the loop, `hero` holds one sheet from the list, not the whole list.
whyWrong.2: Nothing new is made: the loop calls the same function, three times.

questions.explain: Three sheets, three calls, like a teacher calling roll: one name at a time. Each time through the loop, `hero` holds the next sheet, and the call hands that one sheet over. The loops at the bottom of the campaign's code work the same way.

exercises.martu:
Bomb Shell's stat sheet is a [[dictionary]]: you look a value up by its key, like a word in the glossary of a textbook. A sheet inside a sheet reads outside first, like a chapter and then a section. Write three lines, one under each numbered comment. I test your code with a test sheet, a test spell name and a test spell.
Stuck? Type your best try, press Run once, then skip this task and come back to it later. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

items.body:
After Part 1, the unit page shows *Your Readiness Check*: your own misses, each with a link to its lesson. Or find the task or question you missed by its title below. Then try only its twin, the matching task in Form B or Form C, not the whole form. For a question, open that form's questions and answer up to its number: each right answer counts as soon as you check it.

items.title: Explain a line you wrote
items.summary: One question, one click: pick the sentence that says what one line of your mini-boss does.

questions.q: Your mini-boss has a line like this one. Which sentence says what it does?
choices: It works out the mana that is left after the cast, but then keeps it nowhere at all.
It stores the hero's mana on the ward's page, under the ward's key `"mana_cost"`.
It takes the ward's cost from the hero's mana, and stores what is left as the new mana.
It sets the hero's mana to the most mana they can ever hold, minus the ward's cost.

whyWrong.0: The `=` stores the result on the hero's sheet, under `"mana"`. Nothing is lost.
whyWrong.1: The left side of `=` is `hero["mana"]`, the hero's sheet, not the ward's page.
whyWrong.3: `"max_mana"` is not in this line. The right side reads the mana the hero has now.

questions.explain: Python works out the right side first: the hero's mana now, minus the ward's cost. Then `=` stores the answer back under `"mana"` on the hero's sheet, like a new bank balance. In math, x = x − 6 has no answer, but Python's `=` means *gets*.

items.title: Readiness Check · Part 1 · Form B questions
items.summary: Optional. Form B is another version of Part 1, with new names and numbers. Open it when *Mar'tu's Notes: Where to Look Again* sends you here, and do only the task it names. For a question, answer up to its number: each right answer counts as soon as you check it. No hints here. The glossary, read-aloud and the error box in the Console still work.

questions.q: What will the last line print?
questions.explain: `+` glues text like a compound word: sun + flower is sunflower, with no space added. The only space is the one inside `"Shield: "`. `str(mana)` turns the number 5 into the text `5`, so the parentheses and the word `str` never show.

questions.q: `get_farewell()` tidies its line, and the last line prints what it hands back. What will it print?
questions.explain: `.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the very first letter big. It is not like sentence case in Google Docs: names get no capital, so even Lucky's name stays small. Each line stores its result back in `line`.

questions.q: `dodge_check` needs a roll of 14 or more. What will the three `print` lines show?
questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*, like the filled dot on a number line: 14 itself counts. 13 is below 14, so `False`. 14 is exactly enough, so `True`. 15 is more, so `True`. The function hands back the comparison's answer.

questions.q: Trace this program like a ledger: write down what each variable holds, one line at a time, the way you show your work in math. Then type the number it prints.
questions.explain: Trace with the values inside the variables. Here is another call, `armor_score(2, 1) + 3`: `plates` gets 2 and `studs` gets 1, so `heavy` is 2 × 6 = 12 and `light` is 1 × 2 = 2. The function hands back 14, the way f(2) is replaced by its answer in math, and the line adds 3: 17. If you typed 11, you added the numbers written in the function, 6 + 2, then the 3. If you typed 12, you added the numbers handed in, 4 + 5, then the 3.

questions.q: What will this program print?
choices:
Oogrish: Steady, now.
The fire crackles.

Bomb Shell: Shield up.
The fire crackles.

Bomb Shell: Shield up.
Lucky: Fine. I'm in.
The fire crackles.
questions.answer:
Bomb Shell: Shield up.
The fire crackles.
questions.explain: Python asks each question in order, like a grading scale read from the top, and runs only the first branch whose answer is `True`: the `elif`. It skips `else`. The last `print` is not indented, so it is outside the chain and always runs.

questions.q: What will the two `print` lines show?
questions.explain: `in` on a dictionary looks at its keys only, like a glossary: you look up the words, not the definitions. `"Glimmer"` is a key, so `True`. 4 is a value, not a key, so `False`.

questions.q: What will this line print?
questions.explain: `*` with text repeats it, the way 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 in math: four `█`, then three `░`. Then `+` glues them together, with no space added.

questions.q: A d8 is a die with 8 faces. A d8 roll is `random.randint(1, 8)`. Which numbers can it give?

whyWrong.0: A die has no 0 face: the first number, 1, is the lowest it can give.
whyWrong.1: [[randint]] includes its last number, so 8 can come up, like the top face of a real d8.
whyWrong.3: It gives any whole number from the first to the last, not only the two ends.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 8)` gives a whole number from 1 to 8, and both ends can come up. Like a real d8, every face is equally likely.

questions.q: `charms` holds a function under the key `"spark"`. What is the difference between these two lines?
choices: Both lines call the spell, so it runs twice.
The first only reads the function. The second calls it.
The first calls the spell. The second only reads it.
The first reads the text `"spark"`. The second calls it.

whyWrong.0: Only the parentheses on the end call a function, like f(3) in math. Without them, the line only reads what is stored.
whyWrong.2: It is the other way around: the line with `(gearshift)` on the end is the one that calls.
whyWrong.3: `charms["spark"]` is what is stored under the key: the function `spark` itself, not text.

questions.explain: In math class, f names a function and f(3) works it out. In the same way, `charms["spark"]` reads the [[function as a value|function]] stored under the key without running it, and `(gearshift)` on the end runs it on Gearshift, like `spark(gearshift)`.

questions.q: What will this program print?
questions.explain: The line `charms["spark"]` on its own reads the function and does nothing with it, so nothing prints: Python reads it and throws it away. Only `charms["spark"](gearshift)` calls it, so `Gearshift sparks.` shows once.

questions.q: How many times does `check_in` run, and what is it handed each time?
choices: 3 times, with one hero's sheet each time.
3 times, with the whole roster each time.

whyWrong.0: The call is indented under the [[for loop]]. So it runs once each time through the loop, and `member` holds one hero each time.
whyWrong.2: `check_in(member)` hands over `member`, one sheet from the roster, not the whole list.
whyWrong.3: The loop goes through every sheet in `roster`, not only the first.

questions.explain: The loop takes the sheets one at a time, in order, like a teacher calling roll: 3 sheets, so 3 times through. Each time, `member` holds one hero's sheet, and `check_in(member)` hands that one sheet over.

questions.q: Same program. While the loop runs, what does `member` hold?
choices: The text `"member"`, the same every time through the loop.
A count of the times through the loop: 1, then 2, then 3.
Each hero's sheet in turn, one each time through the loop.
The whole roster, all three sheets at once, every time.

whyWrong.0: `member` has no quotes: it is a variable, the [[loop variable]].
whyWrong.1: The loop does not count. It hands over each item of `roster`, in order.
whyWrong.3: The whole roster is `roster`. `member` holds one item of it each time through the loop.

questions.explain: `for member in roster:` puts each item of `roster` in `member`, one at a time, in order, like a teacher calling roll. Each item is a hero's sheet, a [[dictionary]].

checkpoints.text: Make a mage with too little affinity get a message that says why, and no cast.
hints: Look at the mage's `"abilities"`, and at the page's `"required_affinity"`.
Two keys in a row read inside a sheet, the outer key first. *Lower than* is `<`.

Only one branch runs. The lines that must wait for the question move one indent further in, under `else:`. With other names:
```python
if jar["honey"] < spoon["size"]:
    print("Not enough honey.")
else:
    pour(jar, spoon)
```

items.title: Readiness Check · Part 1 · Form C questions
items.summary: Optional. Form C is another version of Part 1, with new names and numbers. Open it when *Mar'tu's Notes: Where to Look Again* sends you here, and do only the task it names. For a question, answer up to its number: each right answer counts as soon as you check it. No hints here. The glossary, read-aloud and the error box in the Console still work.

questions.q: What will the last line of this code print?
questions.explain: `str(ore)` turns the number 8 into the text `8`, so nothing is added up. Then `+` glues the pieces like a compound word, with no spaces added. The only space is the one inside `"Ore: "`.

questions.q: `get_alarm()` tidies its line with `.lower()`, then `.capitalize()`. What will the last line print?
questions.explain: `.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the very first letter big. It is not like sentence case in Google Docs: names get no capital, so even Gearshift's name stays small. Each line stores its result back in `line`.

questions.q: `climb_check` checks a roll against `needed`, which is 16. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*, like the filled dot on a number line: 16 itself counts. 17 is more than 16, so `True`. 16 is exactly enough, so `True`. 15 is short, so `False`. The function hands back the comparison's answer.

questions.q: Trace this program like a ledger: write down what each variable holds, one line at a time, the way you show your work in math. Then type the number it prints.
questions.explain: Here is the same kind of trace for another call, `fuel_burn(1, 3) + 6`. `miles` gets 1 and `loads` gets 3, so `road` is 3 and `haul` is 15. The function hands back 18, and the line adds 6, so it prints 24. Trace yours the same way, with what is *in* the variables, not the numbers written in the function or the numbers handed in.

questions.q: `choice` holds `"option 4"`. What will this code print?
choices:
Oogrish: Wait here.
The wind drops.

Lucky: Not me.
The wind drops.
questions.answer:
Lucky: Not me.
The wind drops.
questions.explain: Python checks the chain from the top, like a grading scale. `choice == "option 1"` is `False`, and `choice == "option 2"` is `False`, so Python runs the line under `else`, which means *otherwise*. The last `print` has no indent, so it is outside the chain and always runs.

questions.q: What will this code print?
questions.explain: `in` on a dictionary looks at its keys only, the way you check a glossary for a word, not for its meaning. 7 is a value, not a key, so `False`. `"Flare"` is a key, so `True`.

questions.q: What will this line of code print?
questions.explain: `*` with text repeats it, the way 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 in math: two `█`, then five `░`. Then `+` glues them together, with no space added.

questions.q: A d12 is a die with 12 faces. Its roll is `random.randint(1, 12)`. Which numbers can it give?
choices: 1 to 11, because the last number is left out
1 to 12, and both 1 and 12 can come up
Only 1 or 12, the two numbers in the parentheses

whyWrong.0: [[randint]] includes its last number, so 12 can come up, like the top face of a real d12.
whyWrong.2: A die has no 0 face: the first number, 1, is the lowest it can give.
whyWrong.3: It gives any whole number from the first to the last, not only the two ends.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 12)` rolls like a fair d12: any whole number from 1 to 12, and both 1 and 12 can come up.

questions.q: `fixes` holds a function under the key `"patch"`. What is the difference between the last two lines?
choices: Both lines run the function, so Bomb Shell is fixed twice.
The first runs the function. The second only reads what is stored under the key.
The first is the text `"patch"`, the key's name. The second runs the function with it.
The first is the function itself, and runs nothing. The second calls it, with `bomb_shell`.

whyWrong.0: Only the parentheses on the end call a function, like f(3) in math. Without them, the line only reads what is stored.
whyWrong.1: It is the other way around: the line with `(bomb_shell)` on the end is the one that calls.
whyWrong.2: `fixes["patch"]` is what is stored under the key: the function `patch` itself, not text.

questions.explain: In math class, f names a function and f(3) works it out. In the same way, `fixes["patch"]` reads the [[function as a value|function]] stored under the key without running it, and `(bomb_shell)` on the end runs it on Bomb Shell, like `patch(bomb_shell)`.

questions.q: Here is the same `fixes` dictionary. What will this code print?
choices:
Bomb Shell is fixed.
Next.
Bomb Shell is fixed.

patch
Next.
Bomb Shell is fixed.
questions.explain: The line `fixes["patch"]` on its own reads the function and does nothing with it, like writing f without (3), so nothing prints. Then `Next.` prints. Only `fixes["patch"](bomb_shell)` calls it, so one more line prints.

questions.q: How many times does `greet` run, and what is it handed each time?
choices: 4 times, with the whole team each time.
4 times, with one hero's sheet each time.

whyWrong.0: The call is indented under the [[for loop]]. So it runs once each time through the loop, and `friend` holds one hero each time.
whyWrong.1: `greet(friend)` hands over `friend`, one sheet from the team, not the whole list.
whyWrong.3: The loop goes through every sheet in `team`, not only the last one.

questions.explain: The loop takes the sheets one at a time, in order, like a teacher calling roll: 4 sheets, so 4 times through. Each time, `friend` holds one hero's sheet, and `greet(friend)` hands that one sheet over.

questions.q: Same program. While the loop runs, what does `friend` hold?
choices: The whole team, all four sheets at once, every time through the loop.
Each hero's sheet in turn: Oogrish's, then Lucky's, then Gearshift's, then Mar'tu's.
The text `"friend"`, the same every time through the loop.
A count of the heroes so far: 1, then 2, then 3, then 4.

whyWrong.0: The whole team is `team`. `friend` holds one item of it each time through the loop.
whyWrong.2: `friend` has no quotes, so it is a variable: the [[loop variable]].
whyWrong.3: The loop does not count the heroes. It hands over each sheet, in order.

questions.explain: `for friend in team:` puts each item of `team` in `friend`, one at a time, in order, like a teacher calling roll. Each item is a hero's sheet, a [[dictionary]].

exercises.martu:
Gearshift's ore gauge works like a mana bar: one `█` for each lump of ore left, then one `░` for each lump burned. Ore is the rock he burns as fuel. Python repeats text the way 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4: `"█" * 3` is `███`. Line 5 is broken, so Python stops. Read the box in the Console, then fix line 5. I test it with other amounts of ore.

checkpoints.text: Fix line 5, so `empty` holds one `░` for each lump of ore burned.

items.title: Readiness Re-check questions
items.summary: The re-check starts here: four questions, with no hints. Get 3 of the 4 right. Then come four short tasks.

questions.q: `lock_check` checks a roll against `needed`, which is 12. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*, like the filled dot on a number line: 12 itself counts. 12 is exactly enough, so `True`. 11 is short, so `False`. 13 is more than enough, so `True`.

questions.q: What will this code print?
questions.explain: `in` on a dictionary looks at its keys only, the way you check a glossary for a word, not for its meaning. 1 is a value, not a key, so `False`. `"Rope"` is a key, so `True`.

questions.q: `moves` holds a function under the key `"hop"`. What is the difference between the last two lines?
choices: The first is the function itself, and runs nothing. The second calls it, with `lucky`.
Both lines run the function, so Lucky hops twice.
The first makes Lucky hop. The second only reads what is stored under the key.
The first is the text `"hop"`, the key's name. The second turns that text into a function.

whyWrong.1: Only the parentheses on the end call a function, like f(3) in math. Without them, the line only reads what is stored.
whyWrong.2: It is the other way around: the line with `(lucky)` on the end is the one that calls.
whyWrong.3: `moves["hop"]` is what is stored under the key: the function `hop` itself, not text.

questions.explain: In math class, f names a function and f(3) works it out. In the same way, `moves["hop"]` reads the [[function as a value|function]] stored under the key without running it, and `(lucky)` on the end runs it on Lucky, like `hop(lucky)`.

questions.q: Here is the same `moves` dictionary. What will this code print?
choices:
Lucky hops.
Set.
Lucky hops.
Lucky hops.
questions.explain: `go = moves["hop"]` stores the function itself in `go`, like giving f a second name, and runs nothing. Then `Set.` prints. Each `go(lucky)` calls it once, so two lines print.

exercises.title: The bar's gap
exercises.martu:
A mana bar shows one `░` for each point of mana used up, like the bars in the campaign. Mana is a hero's magic power, and max mana is the most they can hold. Write the whole function that counts the used-up points. Like a formula in math, it must work for any numbers, not only for one call. The Example shows the shape with its own names, not yours. I test your function with other numbers.
Stuck? Skip this task and come back to it later. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.
